newsitem.title: USA: Germany sees role as east-west mediator.
newsitem.headline: Germany sees role as east-west mediator.

text.p: German President Roman Herzog, describing his country as a mediator between east and west, met U.S. President Bill Clinton on Thursday and said Germany had not yet shaken off the prejudices of the past.

"Obviously in America we always have to make clear that our 50-year-old democracy is a stable democracy and, for example, has relatively little in common with Nazi Germany," he told a news conference during an official visit here.
"We stand by our historical responsibilities, but we insist on the assertion that we are a different country."

Herzog, who visited Washington's graphic Holocaust Museum of Nazi war crimes during his trip to the United States, said the new Germany was winning a role as a mediator between Western states and those of central and eastern Europe and often had to speak out on behalf of those countries.
"We are quite comfortable with that role," he said.
But he said Germany would remain tied to Western Europe and to the NATO Western military alliance, which this month announced plans to admit three new member states.
"I have made it clear that today's Germany is a country of Western Europe and that that will not change," he said.
He said his luncheon meeting with Clinton had gone well. The two men had spoken so much that they barely had time to eat. "I imagine that President Clinton was as hungry as I was when we stood up.

In a written statement, the White House said Clinton and Herzog agreed on the fundamental importance of the partnership between the United States and Germany and reaffirmed their common commitment to the spread of freedom and democracy throughout Europe.
"They also compared efforts in Germany and the United States to enhance opportunities for minorities and promote ethnic tolerance," the statement said.
Herzog, whose post is largely ceremonial, has taken on a role as Germany's moral conscience and and he was the first German president to visit the relatively new Holocaust Museum.
Germany is planning its own memorial to Jews murdered under Hitler's rule and there has been much public debate over exactly what form the monument should take.
